wiki.content: All We Know Is Falling is the debut studio album by American rock band Paramore, released on July 26, 2005 under the Atlantic-distributed Fueled by Ramen in the United States. Its production was led by James Paul Wisner, Mike Green, Nick Trevisick, and Roger Alan Nichols. Josh Farro and Hayley Williams, guitarist and vocalist of Paramore, respectively, wrote almost all the songs. The departure of bassist Jeremy Davis, which occurred a few days after arriving in Orlando, served as the album's main theme. This theme was reflected especially in the album's cover and title. Mostly categorized as a pop punk album, the album received mostly positive reviews and has been labeled a "scene classic". The album's production took place in Orlando, Florida. Instead of making a major push towards radio, the band's A&R recommended that the band build a fanbase through word of mouth. The album received mixed reviews by music journalism, who praised the voice of Hayley Williams. However, the album had a weak domestic commercial performance: it failed to enter the Billboard 200, though it did reach number 30 on Billboard's Heatseekers Chart. The album reached No. 4 on the UK Rock Chart, and in 2010 it managed to reach the place fifty-one the UK Albums Chart and earned certification as a gold record by the BPI. In July 2014, after the group found success with its following records, All We Know Is Falling received gold certification from the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). Three singles from the album were released: "Pressure", "Emergency" and "All We Know". None of the singles managed to reach any major chart, although "Pressure" was certified gold by the RIAA in 2016 after the band found commercial success with subsequent releases. wiki.content: Stadium Arcadium is the ninth studio album by alternative rock band Red Hot Chili Peppers, released on May 9, 2006 via Warner Bros. Records. It sold 442,000 copies in the U.S. in the first week and debuted at number one on the Billboard 200. The album spawned five hit singles: "Dani California", "Snow ((Hey Oh))", "Desecration Smile", "Hump De Bump", and "Tell Me Baby". According to the band's frontman Anthony Kiedis, Stadium Arcadium was originally scheduled to be a trilogy of albums each released six months apart, but was eventually condensed into a double album. Stadium Arcadium was critically praised for integrating musical styles from several aspects of the band's career. The album gained the band seven Grammy Award nominations in 2007 including an award for Best Rock Album. It was the most nominations that the band had garnered in their 25-year career. Kiedis attributed the album's success to less abrasive dynamics within the band, saying that the band's "chemistry when it comes to writing is better than ever. There was always a struggle to dominate lyrically. But we are now confident enough in who we are, so everybody feels more comfortable contributing more and more valuable, quality stuff." After the release of their previous album, By the Way, the Red Hot Chili Peppers embarked on a world tour, which lasted from July 2002 to a mid-June 2004 date at London's Hyde Park. The band later appeared at the 2004 Democratic National Convention and at Rock am Ring to tie up their tour in support of By the Way. The band then settled down to begin recording their next album in September 2004 with producer Rick Rubin, with whom they had recorded four albums previously. The formation and recording of Stadium Arcadium took place at "The Mansion," the former home of Harry Houdini where the Chili Peppers had recorded their 1991 breakthrough Blood Sugar Sex Magik. Given the house's reputation for being "haunted," guitarist John Frusciante recalled that he felt "there were beings of higher intelligence controlling what I was doing, and I didn’t know how to talk about it or explain it...it was very clear to me that the music was coming from somewhere other than me. However, Kiedis noted that during the recording process of the album "everybody was in a good mood. There was very little tension, very little anxiety, very little weirdness going on and every day we showed up to this funky room in the Valley, and everyone felt more comfortable than ever bringing in their ideas." The band originally wanted to create an "old-fashioned Meet the Beatles-like record," and to keep the number of songs down to about 13, to make "a small, digestible piece of art." They ended up writing 38 new songs with Rubin, recording them all. The musical style of the album combines many aspects of music from throughout the band's career, with many fans and critics welcoming the return of the band's signature funk sound after its significant absence from By the Way. It is also noted that John's playing style had changed from his signature 'less is more' style, inspired by punk and new wave guitarists to a more flashy approach, drawing influence from guitarists such as Eddie Van Halen and Steve Vai. While he received moderate acclaim before Stadium Arcadium, this change in style gained him far more recognition than before. John also began utilizing layering in his guitar playing, which is something he had not done before (many layered guitar parts appeared on Mother's Milk, but this was mostly because of the insistence of the producer, although it was against John's will) and also used a modular synthesizer on many songs after doing so on his 2004 album Shadows Collide with People. While John was pleased to have used the modular synthesizer on the album, he admitted that when the band began rehearsing for the tour, it was very frustrating because many of the songs sounded very empty without it. This meant the band had to rework many of the songs in order to perform them live. Kiedis recalled that the band "wanted to on three separate discs that be released in installments...something about those songs made us really like each one. However, by the time we planned to release the third installment in two years, we’ll be writing new music." This was the impetus for the band to pare those songs down to 28, a process Kiedis described as "heartwrenching." All of the 10 unused songs have been released in some form or another (see section on B-sides below). He explained the reasoning behind the decision to name the album "Stadium Arcadium" by saying that it had more "variety and verve compared to its predecessors we each have things we do best and it’s all in there. Everybody played their part and expressed their creativity to the max." Read more on Last.fm. User-contributed text is available under the Creative Commons By-SA License; additional terms may apply.

wiki.content: Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends is the fourth studio album by British band Coldplay, released on June 12, 2008 on the Parlophone label. The album was named after a Spanish phrase that best translates into English as "Long live life". Lyrically, the album contains references to love, life, death and war. Recording sessions for the album took place from June 2007 to April 2008 and featured production by Jon Hopkins, Rik Simpson, Markus Dravs and Brian Eno. The album was Coldplay's first to be produced by Eno, and also their first album to not be produced by long-time Coldplay producer, Ken Nelson. The band forced themselves to explore new styles, as Eno required every song on the album to sound different. Development of the album delayed the release date several times. The album cover of Viva la Vida is the 1830 painting Liberty Leading the People by Eugène Delacroix. Viva la Vida was both a critical and commercial success. It won Best Rock Album at the 2009 Grammy Awards and was also nominated for Album of the Year. It was the best-selling album of 2008. wiki.content: "The Joshua Tree" is the fifth studio album by Irish rock band U2, released March 9, 1987 on Island Records. Recording sessions took place from July to November of 1986 at Windmill Lane Studios in Dublin. The album features the band's exploration of roots rock, with their music exhibiting influences from blues-rock, folk rock, Southern rock, and gospel music. Lyrically, "The Joshua Tree" depicts the band's fascination with America and many of the ideas it stands for. The album was produced and engineered by Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois. The album increased the band's stature "from heroes to superstars," according to Rolling Stone. The album produced several hit singles, including "Where the Streets Have No Name", "With or Without You", and "I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For", all of which remain radio staples. "The Joshua Tree" won Grammy Awards for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal and Album of the Year in Grammy Awards of 1988. In 2003, the album was ranked number 26 on Rolling Stone magazine's list of "The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time". The album is one of the world's best-selling albums of all-time, having sold over 28 million copies. In 2007, a remastered version of the album was released to mark the 20th anniversary of its original release. Following "The Unforgettable Fire" album, U2 realised that they "had no tradition, we were from outer space", and they explored American blues, country and gospel music. Since that album, they had spent time with fellow Irish bands The Waterboys and Hothouse Flowers, and felt a sense of indigenous Irish music being blended with American folk music. Friendships with Bob Dylan, Van Morrison and Keith Richards encouraged the band to look back to the roots of rock music, and focused Bono on his skills as a song and lyric writer. The band wanted to build on "The "Unforgettable Fire"'s atmospherics, but also sought a more hard-hitting sound within the strict discipline of more conventional song structures, in contrast to "The Unforgettable Fire"'s often out-of-focus experimentation. The band interrupted their 1986 album sessions to join Amnesty International's A Conspiracy of Hope Tour. Rather than being a distraction, the band found the tour added extra intensity and power to their new music, providing extra focus on what they wanted to say. The album sessions for "The Joshua Tree" proper began in July 1986 at Windmill Lane Studios in Dublin. In his earlier 1986 travels to Central America, Bono saw first hand the distress of peasants bullied in political conflicts, and this was a central influence on the album. The United States' military intervention in El Salvador angered Bono and prompted him to ask The Edge to "put El Salvador through an amplifier" for the song "Bullet the Blue Sky". "Mothers of the Disappeared" was inspired by the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, the mothers of the thousands of "disappeared" people who opposed the Videla and Galtieri coup d'état that overtook Argentina in 1976, and who were kidnapped and never seen again. The album juxtaposes antipathy towards the United States, including anger at United States foreign policy in Central America, against the band's deep fascination with the country, its open spaces, freedom and what it stood for. The band wanted music with a sense of location, a 'cinematic' quality; its music and lyrics drew on imagery created by American writers the band had been reading. The band had toured in the United States extensively, which affected the band; according to Bono, the album was inspired and influenced more by the country's geography, rather than its people. Bono said he "...had to 'deal with' the United States and the way it was affecting me, because the United States' having such an effect on the world at the moment. On this record I had to deal with it on a political level for the first time, if in a subtle way." Since Bono was trying to portray the both "mythic idea of America" and the "reality of America" on the album, the working title of the album was "The Two Americas". The record was also influenced by the blues. While in recording sessions for the b-side "Silver and Gold", working with Keith Richards, Bono and Richards listened to blues music, country music, American pop music from the 1950s, and other such influences. These influences, combined with Bono's early influences, such as Patti Smith and Bob Dylan, had an effect on the song and the whole album. "Where the Streets Have No Name" was conceived prior to one of the "Joshua Tree" recording sessions by guitarist The Edge. Bono conceived the lyrics with the idea that one could determine a person's religion and income based on where they lived in Belfast. While recording the song as a band, however, U2 ran into difficulty. The song's frequent chord and time changes caused problems in playing the song correctly; the difficulty was so great that producer Brian Eno attempted to erase the track. Drummer Larry Mullen Jr. later said of the song, "It took so long to get that song right, it was difficult for us to make any sense of it. It only became a truly great song through playing live. On the record, musically, it's not half the song it is live." "I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For" grew from another song called "Under the Weather Girls", which co-producer Daniel Lanois didn't like, except for Larry Mullen, Jr.'s drum track and Adam Clayton's bass line. These parts were used as the foundation of "I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For". The development of the song saw the addition of such things as a subtle auto-pan effect added to one of The Edge's guitar overdubs and Bono, a tenor, singing in the upper register of his range to add to the feeling of spiritual yearning. Both Bono and Edge have, in fact, called it a gospel song on numerous occasions. "With or Without You", the album's first single and one of the band's most well-known songs, uses an effect called "infinite guitar", developed by Michael Brook, to infinitely sustain notes. The band concluded recording of the album in November 1986. A number of songs that were released as B-sides to singles from "The Joshua Tree" are thought to have been considered for a double-album version of The Joshua Tree. Though Bono was the most vocal proponent of this extended version of the album, The Edge successfully argued for the 11-track version that was ultimately released. "Spanish Eyes" and "Deep in the Heart" were released as B-sides to the "I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For" single. "Luminous Times (Hold on to Love)" and "Walk to the Water" were released as B-sides to the "With or Without You" single. "Sweetest Thing", "Silver and Gold", and "Race Against Time" were released as B-sides to the "Where the Streets Have No Name" single. "The Joshua Tree" was first released on 9 March 1987. The album cover photo was taken by Dutch photographer Anton Corbijn in December 1986. Corbijn later recounted the photo shoot in Death Valley, California; "This is the most serious set of shots I have taken of U2 and they became my most well-known photographs at the time. It was taken with a panoramic camera to take more of the landscapes in which was the main idea of the shoot: man and environment, the Irish in America." In 2007, a 20th anniversary edition of the album was released, featuring remastered tracks, along with B-sides and rarities. Four different formats of the remaster were made available. "With or Without You" and the rhythmic gospel "I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For" were released as singles internationally and quickly went to #1 in the U.S. "Where the Streets Have No Name" was also successfully released. "In God's Country" was released as a fourth single in North America with modest success, while "One Tree Hill" was released as a fourth single in Australia and New Zealand. Initially slated as a single release, "Red Hill Mining Town" was the only track from the album not played on the tour. Bono has suggested that the song's high notes put too much strain on his voice. Upon its release, "The Joshua Tree" debuted at #1 in the UK and also quickly reached the top of the charts in the U.S. U2 became the fourth rock band to be featured on the cover of Time magazine (following The Beatles, The Band, and The Who), who declared that U2 was "Rock's Hottest Ticket". The album brought U2 to a new level of mega-stardom, as the worldwide Joshua Tree Tour sold out arenas and stadiums around the world, the first time the band had consistently played venues of that size. "The Joshua Tree" won U2 their first two Grammy Awards, with the band receiving honors for "Album of the Year" and "Best Rock Performance By a Duo or Group With Vocal". According to U.S. Recording Industry sales figures, as of January 2005, "The Joshua Tree" ranks as the 89th best-selling album of all-time in the U.S. and, as of 2006, the 26th best-selling album in the U.K.. The album has sold 10 million copies in the United States alone and more than 25 million copies worldwide. It remains the band's best-selling album. "The Joshua Tree" is often cited as one of the greatest albums in rock history. In 1989, it was rated #3 on Rolling Stone magazine's list of "The 100 Greatest Albums of the 80's", as well as appearing at #26 on the magazine's "500 Greatest Albums of All Time". The Definitive 200 list sponsored by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame ranks the album as the fifth-greatest in history. "The Joshua Tree" was selected as #6 on CCM Magazine's 2001 list of the greatest Contemporary Christian music albums of all time (see CCM Presents: The 100 Greatest Albums in Christian Music). It came second place in Channel 4's 100 Greatest albums. It came in at #10 on ABC Television's My Favourite Album program, which aired in Australia in December 2006. Read more on Last.fm. wiki.content: The Bends, released on 13 March 1995 in the United Kingdom and on 4 April 1995 in the United States, is the second studio album released by the English rock band Radiohead. The album was dedicated to the late comedian Bill Hicks. The album contains singles "High and Dry", "Fake Plastic Trees", "Just", "My Iron Lung", and "Street Spirit (Fade Out)". The Bends was ranked number 110 on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time, and number 2 on Q's 100 Greatest Albums Ever. The album was subject to much greater critical acclaim than their debut Pablo Honey (1993), and it reached number four in the UK Albums Chart. However, it failed to build on the commercial success of their single "Creep" outside the United Kingdom, and it peaked on the American charts at number 88. Although it lacked the instant success of later Radiohead albums, The Bends achieved triple platinum sales certifications in the UK and Canada and platinum sales in the US and the EU. According to the band, The Bends marked the start of a gradual turn in Yorke's songwriting from personal angst to the more cryptic lyrics and social and global themes that would come to dominate the band's later work. Most of the album was seen to continue the lyrical concerns of Pablo Honey, although in more mature fashion. The songs "Fake Plastic Trees" and, in particular, "Street Spirit (Fade Out)" and its b-side "Talk Show Host", are often seen as a precursor to their next album OK Computer (1997). "Fake Plastic Trees" was partly inspired by the commercial development of Canary Wharf, while "Sulk" was written as a response to the Hungerford massacre. According to Yorke, "Street Spirit (Fade Out)" was inspired by the book The Famished Road by Ben Okri. The lyrics to the songs on The Bends, particularly those of "My Iron Lung", were cited in the British music press as an example of Yorke's alleged depression. Melody Maker ran an article during The Bends period which suggested Yorke would be the next "rock 'n roll martyr" or suicide. The Bends was the first of the band's full-length records with artwork by Stanley Donwood, in collaboration with Yorke, who went under the name "The White Chocolate Farm" (later shortened to Tchock). Originally Yorke had wanted to use an image of an iron lung as the cover, but he lost it. The eventual album cover was created at the last minute by morphing a photograph taken by Donwood of a medical dummy with Yorke's own face. It is also the last Radiohead album whose liner notes and artwork include pictures of the band members. The Bends met with much greater critical acclaim than Pablo Honey, appearing on many end-of-year lists in 1995. Within the UK, it assured Radiohead's role as a standard-bearer of "indie" Brit-rock bands. The album was released during the height of the '90s Britpop movement, benefiting from renewed press attention to British guitar music; however, in the band's home country, Radiohead's music was rarely grouped with Blur, Pulp and other so-called "Britpop" acts, instead receiving some acclaim for diverging from the fashionable aspects of the scene. In the United States, the album eventually reached number 88 on the Billboard 200 in 1996, while the single "High and Dry" reached number 78 on the Billboard Hot 100. In the UK, The Bends reached number 4 and remains a bestseller. In mid-1995 Radiohead toured as an opening act for R.E.M., playing songs from The Bends and extending their popularity with a mass audience. The Bends had an influence on the subsequent generation of British pop bands. In 2006, The Observer listed it as one of "the 50 albums that changed music", saying, "Radiohead's Thom Yorke popularised the angst-laden falsetto, a thoughtful opposite to the chest-beating lad-rock personified by Oasis's Liam Gallagher. Singing in a higher octave-range and falsetto voice to a backdrop of churning guitars became a much-copied idea, however, one that eventually coalesced into an entire decade of sound. Without this, Coldplay would not exist, nor Keane, nor James Blunt." Radiohead members said they later distanced themselves from their mid '90s sound partly because they felt little affinity for those that adopted the sound. The Bends took second place behind Radiohead's OK Computer in both 1998 and 2006 reader polls of Q magazine for the best album of all time. In 2003, the album was ranked number 110 on Rolling Stone's list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. Rolling Stone initially gave the album an average rating. In 2000, Virgin's Top 1000 Albums of All Time ranked The Bends at number two, second only to Revolver by The Beatles. Read more on Last.fm. "The Beatles", commonly known as "The White Album", is the ninth studio album and only double album by the English rock band the Beatles. It was released on 22 November 1968 and was the band's first album issued by Apple Records. The cover features a plain white sleeve with the band's name embossed on it, contrasting with the elaborate artwork of their previous album, "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band" (1967). The album contains 30 tracks spanning a wide range of styles, including rock and roll, folk, country, blues, ska, music hall, hard rock and avant-garde music. Its diverse musical approach and fragmented structure have led some critics to interpret it as a postmodern work. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest albums of all time.

The Beatles began recording the album at EMI Studios in London in late May 1968, with sessions continuing until mid-October. The recording period was marked by disagreements over musical direction and the presence of John Lennon's partner, Yoko Ono, who regularly attended sessions despite the band's previous practice of generally excluding spouses and partners. Producer George Martin took an unannounced holiday during the sessions, leaving his assistant Chris Thomas to oversee some of the production. Recording engineer Geoff Emerick left during a session in July because of the tension within the group. In August, drummer Ringo Starr temporarily left the band for two weeks. These difficulties continued into the following year, preceding the band's eventual break-up.

Nineteen of the album's 30 songs were written during the Beatles' visit to Rishikesh, India, between February and April 1968, where they attended a Transcendental Meditation course led by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. The retreat provided an opportunity for the band members to write songs away from their usual professional commitments. Lennon and Paul McCartney frequently met to review their new compositions, while George Harrison resumed his focus on guitar after studying the sitar for approximately two years. Musicologist Walter Everett has compared Harrison's development as a songwriter in 1968 with that of Lennon and McCartney earlier in the decade, noting that Harrison produced a substantial amount of material despite his relatively limited role in the group's songwriting.

Starr left the retreat less than two weeks after arriving, citing difficulties with the food, and McCartney departed in mid-March. Harrison and Lennon remained until April. Lennon left after hearing allegations that the Maharishi had behaved inappropriately towards women accompanying the Beatles. McCartney and Harrison later concluded that the allegations were unfounded, and Lennon's wife, Cynthia, stated that there was no evidence to support them.

The band composed approximately 40 songs during the retreat, of which 26 were recorded as demos at Harrison's home, Kinfauns, in Esher, Surrey, in May 1968. Lennon wrote most of the new material, contributing 14 songs. Lennon and McCartney brought home-recorded demos to the recording sessions, and some of the recordings from Rishikesh and Kinfauns were later released on "Anthology 3" in 1996. The complete collection of Esher demos was released in the 2018 deluxe edition commemorating the album's 50th anniversary.

The Beatles was recorded between 30 May and 14 October 1968, primarily at Abbey Road Studios in London, with some sessions at Trident Studios. The atmosphere at the studio differed considerably from the retreat in India, as the band members increasingly pursued separate musical interests and disagreed over arrangements and recording methods. The formation of Apple Corps, the band's multimedia company, also placed financial and organisational demands on the group.

The Beatles booked extended studio time at Abbey Road through July. Rather than relying exclusively on rehearsed backing tracks, the band frequently recorded rehearsals and improvisations before selecting performances for overdubbing. This approach contributed to the album's relatively restrained production, which relied less on elaborate studio experimentation than "Revolver" (1966) and "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band". Harrison's song "Not Guilty" was excluded despite the recording of 102 takes.

Only 16 of the album's 30 tracks feature all four Beatles performing. Several songs were recorded by individual members or by smaller combinations of the group, with songwriters often performing their own instrumental parts. Lennon and McCartney sometimes worked simultaneously in separate studios with different engineers. During the sessions, Abbey Road moved from four-track to eight-track recording. The band initially recorded "Hey Jude" and "Dear Prudence" at Trident Studios, which already had an eight-track recording system. After learning that EMI also possessed such a machine, engineers Ken Scott and Dave Harries installed it in Abbey Road's Studio 2 without the studio management's authorisation.

The album's final mixing and sequencing involved a 24-hour session attended by Lennon, McCartney and Martin. Harrison had travelled to the United States the previous day. Unlike most contemporary LPs, the album was mastered without the customary three-second gaps between tracks. Several songs flow directly into one another through edits, crossfades or incidental musical passages.

The album encompasses a wider range of musical styles than many of the Beatles' previous releases. Its genres include rock and roll, blues, folk, country, reggae, avant-garde, hard rock and music hall. Because the only Western instrument available to the group during their stay in India was the acoustic guitar, many of the songs originated on that instrument. Several retained their acoustic arrangements on the album and were recorded by one member or a small part of the group, including "Wild Honey Pie", "Blackbird", "Julia", "I Will" and "Mother Nature's Son".

Author Nicholas Schaffner interpreted the album's acoustic emphasis as part of a broader move away from the psychedelia associated with 1967, a change also evident in the work of Bob Dylan and the Beach Boys and adopted by artists such as the Rolling Stones and the Byrds in 1968. Music critic Edwin Faust argued that the album's tracks generally remain within their chosen genres, rather than combining several styles within individual songs as the Beatles had increasingly done on earlier releases.

Martin opposed the idea of releasing a double album and suggested reducing the material to a single LP containing the strongest songs. The band rejected the proposal. Harrison later suggested that some tracks could have been issued as B-sides or omitted, while also supporting the double album as a way to accommodate the group's growing collection of songs. Starr proposed dividing the material into two separate albums, which he jokingly called "The White Album" and "The Whiter Album". McCartney defended the decision to release the material as a double album.

During the recording sessions, the Beatles increasingly asserted their individual artistic identities. McCartney later described the period as a turning point for the group, citing the friction among its members. Lennon also stated that the band's eventual break-up could be heard in the album. Emerick, who had worked with the Beatles since "Revolver", became increasingly dissatisfied with the working atmosphere. During the recording of "Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da", he heard Martin criticise McCartney's vocal performance, prompting McCartney to challenge Martin to sing the part himself. On 16 July, Emerick announced that he would no longer work with the band and left the studio during a session.

Ono's presence at the sessions marked a departure from the Beatles' earlier working practices. She accompanied Lennon to Abbey Road during the recording of "Revolution 1" and became a regular presence in the studio. Her involvement affected the group's internal dynamics, particularly the working relationship between Lennon and McCartney. McCartney's girlfriend, Francie Schwartz, also attended some sessions, as did Harrison's wife, Pattie Harrison, and Starr's wife, Maureen Starkey.

Writer Peter Doggett argued that Ono's presence disrupted communication between Lennon and McCartney. Biographer Philip Norman also described the pair as increasingly dismissive of each other's compositions. Harrison and Starr temporarily distanced themselves from the project, travelling to California on 7 June so Harrison could appear in "Raga", a documentary about Indian musician Ravi Shankar. The members' separate artistic projects during 1968 provided further evidence of their growing independence. Lennon and Ono's experimental album "Unfinished Music No. 1: Two Virgins", whose cover depicted the couple nude, also drew criticism and bewilderment from Lennon's bandmates.

On 20 August, Lennon and Starr recorded overdubs for "Yer Blues" in Studio 3 before visiting McCartney, who was working on "Mother Nature's Son" in Studio 2. Engineer Ken Scott later recalled that the atmosphere deteriorated sharply when the three musicians met. Starr left the studio on 22 August during the recording of "Back in the U.S.S.R.", feeling that his contribution to the group was undervalued and objecting to McCartney's criticism of his drumming. McCartney played drums on "Dear Prudence", while Lennon, McCartney and Harrison contributed bass and drums to "Back in the U.S.S.R.". The drum part on the latter track combines performances by all three. Lennon, McCartney and Harrison asked Starr to return, and he rejoined the group on 5 September. Harrison had decorated Starr's drum kit with flowers as a welcome-back gesture.

"The Beatles" was the band's final album to receive separate stereo and mono mixes. Official mono mixes exist for all but two tracks, "Revolution 1" and "Revolution 9", whose mono versions were derived directly from the stereo masters. Several songs differ in length or contain different overdubs and effects between the two mixes. The mono version of "Helter Skelter", for example, omits the fade-in at the end of the song and Starr's concluding shout, while the mono mix of "Yer Blues" has a fade-out 11 seconds longer than the stereo version.

By the time of the album's release in the United States, mono records were being phased out, and the American edition was the Beatles' first LP issued only in stereo. In the United Kingdom, "Yellow Submarine", released in January 1969, was the band's final album to be issued in mono. The mono version of "The Beatles" was made available internationally in September 2009 as part of "The Beatles in Mono" CD box set. The original mono LP was reissued worldwide in September 2014.

"Back in the U.S.S.R." was written by McCartney as a parody of Chuck Berry's "Back in the U.S.A." and the Beach Boys' musical style. The recording opens with a sound effect of an aeroplane taking off and landing, which recurs throughout the track. Lennon and Harrison provided backing vocals influenced by the Beach Boys. The idea of referring to women in the Soviet Union came from Beach Boys member Mike Love, who had suggested the concept while in Rishikesh. The song circulated widely as a bootleg in the Soviet Union, where Beatles recordings were banned, and became popular through unofficial distribution.

"Dear Prudence" was recorded at Trident Studios and features an acoustic guitar arrangement characteristic of songs written during the Indian retreat. Lennon wrote it about Prudence Farrow, actress Mia Farrow's sister, who spent much of the retreat meditating in her room.

"Glass Onion" was the first full-band backing track recorded after Starr's temporary departure. Lennon wrote its lyrics partly to mock listeners who searched Beatles songs for hidden messages. The lyrics refer to other songs in the band's catalogue, including "I Am the Walrus" and "The Fool on the Hill". McCartney added a recorder part following the reference to "The Fool on the Hill", and a string section was recorded in October.

"Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da" was written by McCartney as a pastiche of ska. The recording process was prolonged by McCartney's insistence on repeated attempts to achieve the desired performance. Jimmy Scott, a friend of McCartney's, suggested the title and played bongos on an early take. Scott sought a share of the song's publishing royalties, but the composition was credited to Lennon-McCartney. After three days of work on the original backing track, the band discarded it and began recording a replacement. Lennon disliked the song and described it dismissively, while engineer Richard Lush recalled that Starr was frustrated by repeatedly recording the same part. McCartney attempted a third version, but the band ultimately used the second recording. The group did not release the song as a single in Britain or the United States. A cover version by Marmalade later reached number one on the UK Singles Chart.

McCartney recorded "Wild Honey Pie" on 20 August, at the end of the session for "Mother Nature's Son". The track reflects the short musical fragments he recorded between takes during the album sessions.

"The Continuing Story of Bungalow Bill" was written by Lennon after an American visitor to Rishikesh left the retreat for several weeks to hunt tigers. The recording features vocals by several people present in the studio, including Ono, who sings one line and shares another. Chris Thomas played the Mellotron, including improvised parts at the end of the track. The opening flamenco guitar passage came from a recording in the Mellotron's standard tape library.

Harrison wrote "While My Guitar Gently Weeps" during a visit to his parents' home in Cheshire. He first recorded it as a solo acoustic performance on 25 July, a version later released on "Anthology 3". Dissatisfied with the band's initial attempts to record the song, Harrison invited his friend Eric Clapton to play lead guitar. Clapton was initially reluctant to appear on a Beatles recording, but Harrison insisted that the decision was his to make as the song's writer. Clapton's guitar solo was processed using automatic double tracking. He gave Harrison the guitar used in the recording, which Harrison later named "Lucy".

"Happiness Is a Warm Gun" was assembled from several song fragments that Lennon combined into a single composition. He had previewed two sections in his May 1968 demo. The backing track required 95 takes, partly because of the song's changing time signatures and musical styles. The final version was edited together from portions of two takes. Lennon later identified it as one of his favourite Beatles songs. The recording process was regarded by the band as an opportunity to refine their ensemble playing. Apple press officer Derek Taylor contributed to the lyrics without receiving a songwriting credit.

"Martha My Dear" was named after McCartney's Old English Sheepdog, although the lyrics are unrelated to the animal. McCartney performed the song with session musicians, without contributions from the other Beatles. Martin arranged the brass parts.

"I'm So Tired" was written in India while Lennon was experiencing difficulty sleeping. Recorded during the same session as "The Continuing Story of Bungalow Bill", it includes a reference to Walter Raleigh, whom Lennon criticises for introducing tobacco to Europe. The track ends with Lennon muttering, "Monsieur, monsieur, how about another one?" The phrase later became associated with the "Paul is dead" conspiracy theory, whose proponents claimed that reversing the recording revealed a reference to McCartney's supposed death.

"Blackbird" features McCartney singing and accompanying himself on acoustic guitar. The ticking sound heard in the background has been identified by some accounts as a metronome, while Emerick recalled recording the sound of McCartney's shoes. The birdsong was taken from Abbey Road Studios' sound-effects collection and recorded using an early EMI portable tape recorder.

Harrison wrote "Piggies" as a criticism of greed and materialism in modern society. His mother and Lennon helped complete the lyrics. Thomas played harpsichord, and Lennon supplied a tape loop of pigs grunting.

"Rocky Raccoon" developed from a jam session involving McCartney, Lennon and Donovan during the Indian retreat. The song was recorded in a single session. Martin considered it a comparatively weak track that had been included partly because the album was a double LP.

"Don't Pass Me By" was Starr's first solo composition recorded by the Beatles. He had been considering writing a personal song for several years, and the composition was known during development as "Ringo's Tune" and "This Is Some Friendly". The basic track features Starr on drums and McCartney on piano. Martin wrote an orchestral introduction that was ultimately rejected, and country fiddle player Jack Fallon contributed a bluegrass-style part instead.

McCartney wrote "Why Don't We Do It in the Road?" after observing two monkeys mating in the street in India. He wondered why humans did not behave in a similarly uninhibited manner. McCartney performed all the instruments except drums, which Starr played. Lennon later expressed annoyance that he had not been invited to participate. McCartney suggested that this was reciprocal, as Lennon had not contributed to "Revolution 9".

"I Will" was written and sung by McCartney, with Lennon and Starr contributing percussion. During breaks in the recording session, the three musicians performed other songs. A fragment known as "Can You Take Me Back?" was included between "Cry Baby Cry" and "Revolution 9". Recordings of Cilla Black's "Step Inside Love" and the improvised song "Los Paranoias" were later released on "Anthology 3".

"Julia" was the final track recorded for the album. It features Lennon performing alone on acoustic guitar and is the only Beatles song on which he is the sole performer. Lennon wrote it as a tribute to his mother, Julia Lennon, who died in a road accident in 1958 when he was 17. The lyrics address his grief over her death and his relationship with Ono, referred to as the "ocean child". Ono helped with the lyrics, but the song retained the Lennon-McCartney songwriting credit.

McCartney described "Birthday" as a composition written jointly with Lennon and recorded on the same evening. They were inspired by a British television screening of the rock and roll film "The Girl Can't Help It" and performed the lead vocals in a style influenced by the film's star, Little Richard. Ono and Pattie Harrison added backing vocals after the main recording.

Lennon wrote "Yer Blues" in India, where he continued to experience unhappiness despite the retreat's emphasis on meditation. The lyrics reflect his state of mind. The musical style was influenced by the British blues revival of 1968, associated with bands and musicians including Fleetwood Mac, Cream, the Jimi Hendrix Experience, Jeff Beck and Chicken Shack. The backing track was recorded in a small room adjacent to Abbey Road's Studio 2 control room. The four-track tape was edited directly, creating an abrupt transition into another take before the fade-out.

McCartney wrote "Mother Nature's Son" in India and developed it separately from the other band members. He performed the song alone, accompanied by a brass arrangement written by Martin.

"Everybody's Got Something to Hide Except Me and My Monkey" developed from a jam session and initially had no title. The final mix was created by speeding up the tape, which had been recorded at 43 hertz rather than the usual 50. Harrison stated that the title originated from a saying by the Maharishi, with the phrase "and my monkey" added later.

"Sexy Sadie" was originally written under the title "Maharishi" shortly after Lennon decided to leave Rishikesh. In a 1980 interview, Lennon acknowledged that the Maharishi had inspired the song, explaining that he had changed the name to "Sexy Sadie".

"Helter Skelter" was written by McCartney and initially recorded in July as a blues-oriented piece. The early takes included extended instrumental improvisations and were considered too long for practical inclusion on an LP. The band returned to the song in September and recorded a shorter version. Accounts of the session describe a chaotic atmosphere. Harrison reportedly ran around the studio holding a flaming ashtray above his head, imitating musician Arthur Brown. The stereo version runs nearly a minute longer than the mono version and ends with Starr shouting, "I've got blisters on my fingers!" The song later became associated with Charles Manson, who interpreted it as a reference to an apocalyptic conflict. Manson's interpretation of the song contributed to his belief that the album contained coded messages about an impending race war and influenced the name of his movement.

Harrison's "Long, Long, Long" closes the third side of the album. Its chord progression was partly derived from Bob Dylan's "Sad Eyed Lady of the Lowlands". Music critic Ian MacDonald interpreted the song as expressing reconciliation with God. The basic track was recorded during a lengthy session that began on the afternoon of 7 October and continued until 7 am the following morning. McCartney played Hammond organ. A rattling sound at the end was created when a note caused a wine bottle placed on top of the organ's Leslie speaker to resonate.

"Revolution 1" was the first song recorded for the album, with backing-track sessions beginning on 30 May. The early recordings were intended as possible candidates for a single, but the arrangement became slower and more relaxed as the sessions progressed. The selected take originally ended with a six-minute improvisation, which received additional overdubs before being shortened for the album. A brass arrangement was added later.

McCartney wrote "Honey Pie" as a pastiche of 1920s dance music. The opening was processed to resemble an old 78-rpm record, and Martin arranged saxophone and clarinet parts in a similar style. Lennon played the guitar solo but later expressed dislike for the song.

"Savoy Truffle" was named after a type of chocolate in a box of Mackintosh's Good News, which Clapton enjoyed eating. The recording features a six-piece saxophone section arranged by Thomas, who also played keyboards. Harrison later said that Derek Taylor helped him complete the lyrics.

Lennon began writing "Cry Baby Cry" in late 1967. Some of the lyrics were derived from the tagline of an old television advertisement. Martin played harmonium on the recording.

"Revolution 9" developed from the overdubs recorded for the coda of "Revolution 1". Lennon, Harrison and Ono added tape loops, spoken-word excerpts and other sound collages, drawing on experimental techniques associated with composer Karlheinz Stockhausen. The track opens with an excerpt from a piano performance recorded for a Royal Schools of Music examination tape and includes Ono speaking the phrase "if you become naked". Ono played a substantial role in its production and advised Lennon on the selection of tape loops. McCartney was outside the country during the recording and did not participate, although he had previously led similar experimental projects, including "Carnival of Light" in 1967. "Revolution 9" has remained one of the album's most controversial tracks, attracting both interest and criticism.

Lennon wrote "Good Night" as a lullaby for his son Julian and intended Starr to sing the lead vocal. Early versions featured Lennon on acoustic guitar accompanying Starr. Martin subsequently arranged an orchestral and choral accompaniment that replaced the guitar in the final mix. Martin also played the celesta.

"Hey Jude" was recorded in late July 1968 during the album sessions but released as a separate single nearly three months before the album appeared. It was the first single issued by Apple Records and became the Beatles' most successful single in the United States. Its B-side, "Revolution", was a faster and more heavily distorted version of the song than the album track "Revolution 1". Lennon had wanted the original recording to be released as a single, but the other members considered it too slow. The single version features an electric piano solo by Nicky Hopkins.

In Britain and the United States, the music industry generally treated singles and albums as separate releases and avoided including the same songs on both. Consequently, no singles were taken from "The Beatles" in either country. However, "Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da", backed with "While My Guitar Gently Weeps", was released as a single in several other markets. It reached number one in Australia and achieved commercial success in Japan, Austria and Switzerland.

Several songs developed during the album sessions were later revisited for subsequent Beatles albums or released on the members' solo records. Lennon's "Look at Me" and "Child of Nature", the latter later rewritten as "Jealous Guy", originated during this period, as did McCartney's "Junk" and Harrison's "Not Guilty" and "Circles". Harrison gave "Sour Milk Sea" to singer Jackie Lomax, whose recording was released as a single on Apple Records in August 1968. Lennon's "Mean Mr. Mustard" and "Polythene Pam" were later incorporated into the medley on "Abbey Road" (1969).

Lennon's "What's the New Mary Jane" was demoed at Kinfauns and formally recorded during the album sessions by Lennon, Harrison and Ono. McCartney recorded demos of "Etcetera" and "The Long and Winding Road" at Abbey Road. The latter song was recorded by the Beatles in 1969 for "Let It Be". The band's recordings of "Not Guilty" and "What's the New Mary Jane", along with a demo of "Junk", were released on "Anthology 3". A ten-minute recording known as "Revolution (Take 20)" circulated as a bootleg in 2009. It was subsequently understood to contain material that was edited and overdubbed to produce "Revolution 1" and "Revolution 9".

"The Beatles" was released in the United Kingdom on 22 November 1968 and in the United States three days later. It was the third album issued by Apple Records, following Harrison's "Wonderwall Music" and Lennon's and Ono's "Unfinished Music No. 1: Two Virgins". The album was commonly referred to as "The White Album" from the time of its release.

The cover was designed by conceptual artist Richard Hamilton in collaboration with McCartney. Its plain white sleeve contrasted with the colourful artwork of "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band", designed by Peter Blake and Jann Haworth. The band's name was embossed in Helvetica lettering slightly below the centre of the sleeve's right side. Some later US vinyl editions displayed the title in grey printed letters rather than embossed text.

Each original copy of the album received a unique stamped serial number. Hamilton described the numbering as an ironic treatment of a mass-produced record as a limited edition. The first four numbered copies were given to the band members, making number 0000005 the first publicly sold copy. In 2008, a copy bearing that number sold on eBay for £19,201. In 2015, Starr's copy, numbered 0000001, sold at auction for $790,000, setting a record for a music album at the time. Members of the band Hotline TNT later stated that musician Jack White had purchased the copy, which was held at the headquarters of Third Man Records in Nashville.

The packaging included a poster featuring a photographic collage, with the lyrics printed on the reverse, as well as four photographic portraits taken by John Kelly. Hamilton and McCartney assembled and rearranged the photographs over several days before deciding on the final layout. During production, the album was provisionally titled "A Doll's House", but the name was changed after the English progressive rock band Family released "Music in a Doll's House" earlier in 1968.

In the United Kingdom, "The Beatles" entered the album chart at number one on 7 December 1968 and remained there for seven weeks. It was replaced at the top by "Best of the Seekers" on 25 January 1969, but returned to number one the following week for an eighth and final week. The album spent a total of 22 weeks on the UK chart, considerably fewer than the 149 weeks achieved by "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band". In September 2013, following changes to the British Phonographic Industry's sales award rules, the album was certified platinum, representing sales of at least 300,000 copies.

In the United States, Capitol Records shipped more than 3.3 million copies to retailers during the first four days after release. The album entered the Billboard 200 at number 11 on 14 December 1968, rose to number two and reached number one on 28 December. It spent nine weeks at the top of the chart and a total of 215 weeks on the Billboard 200. According to the Recording Industry Association of America, the album has been certified 24-times platinum in the United States, representing shipments of 24 million units.

The album received predominantly favourable reviews upon release, although some critics objected to its length or argued that it lacked the adventurous production of "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band". Author Ian Inglis noted that both positive and negative assessments frequently focused on the album's fragmented structure, with some critics viewing its stylistic variety as a weakness and others considering it central to the album's identity.

In The Observer, Tony Palmer praised Lennon and McCartney's songwriting and argued that the album challenged cultural snobbery and bourgeois prejudice. Richard Goldstein of The New York Times described the double album as a major achievement, citing its songwriting and reduced reliance on studio effects compared with "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band" and "Magical Mystery Tour". Derek Jewell of The Sunday Times called it the best pop release since "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band", highlighting its range of musical expression. Although he criticised "Revolution 9" as pretentious, NME reviewer Alan Smith praised much of the album. Rolling Stone editor Jann Wenner described it as a synthesis of Western music and considered it the Beatles' strongest album to date.

Other reviewers were less enthusiastic. A Time magazine critic argued that the album displayed both the band's strengths and weaknesses, describing the performances as sophisticated but questioning the collection's sense of taste and purpose. William Mann of The Times criticised Lennon and McCartney's reliance on pastiche and private jokes, although he considered the album an important musical release. In The New York Times, Nik Cohn described the album as tedious and considered more than half its songs mediocre. In a 1971 column for The Village Voice, Robert Christgau called it both the band's most consistent and probably their worst album, characterising the songs as musical exercises. Nevertheless, he ranked it tenth among the albums of 1968 in the annual critics' poll conducted by Jazz & Pop magazine.

Retrospective assessments have continued to reflect differing views of the album's coherence and quality. In a 2003 review for Mojo, Ian MacDonald noted that the album frequently appeared among critics' lists of the greatest albums of all time, but described it as eccentric, highly diverse and inconsistent in quality. Rob Sheffield, writing in "The Rolling Stone Album Guide" in 2004, praised some of its strongest songs while criticising other tracks as self-indulgent filler. Christopher Scapelliti, writing for "MusicHound Rock" in 1999, similarly described the album as self-indulgent and occasionally difficult to listen to, while highlighting "While My Guitar Gently Weeps", "Happiness Is a Warm Gun" and "Helter Skelter".

Eric Henderson of Slant Magazine argued that the album's fragmented character had helped it resist automatic canonisation and remain fresh for later listeners. AllMusic critic Stephen Thomas Erlewine observed that its stylistic diversity could make it seem either scattered or compelling, depending on the listener's perspective, but concluded that the album developed a distinctive identity from its apparent inconsistencies.

Reviews of the 2009 remastered edition were generally positive. Neil McCormick of The Daily Telegraph argued that even the weaker songs functioned within the context of the album's eclectic approach and described it as one of the greatest albums ever made. Mark Kemp of Paste rejected the interpretation that the record consisted of three solo projects and a single Starr composition, arguing that the diversity of the members' ideas strengthened the album. Chuck Klosterman of The A.V. Club gave it a highly favourable assessment. In 2020, Christgau maintained that the album remained somewhat scattered but deserved a high grade. John O'Reilly of The Guardian offered a contrasting assessment, arguing that the material could have been reduced to a stronger single album.

In 2000, "The Beatles" was ranked fifth in the third edition of Colin Larkin's "All Time Top 1000 Albums". In 2003, Rolling Stone placed it tenth on its list of the 500 Greatest Albums of All Time, a position it retained in the 2012 revision. In 2008, the Vatican newspaper L'Osservatore Romano described the album as a collection of 30 songs containing several enduring highlights. Kerrang! ranked it 49th on its 2011 list of the 50 heaviest albums, citing the guitar work on "Helter Skelter". The album was also included in the book "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die". In September 2020, Rolling Stone ranked it 29th on its revised list of the 500 Greatest Albums of All Time.

Giles Martin, son of George Martin and supervisor of the album's 2018 50th-anniversary remix, said that listening to the demos and session recordings had led him to question the common interpretation that the Beatles were on the verge of breaking up during the album's recording. <a href="https://www.last.fm/music/The+Beatles/The+Beatles">Read more on Last.fm</a>. At the 43rd Annual Grammy Awards, the album was nominated for Best Rock Album, and the song "Guerrilla Radio" received the award for Best Hard Rock Performance. In year-end rankings, both Time and Rolling Stone listed the album among their top releases of 1999. The album was certified double platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America, indicating sales of at least two million units in the United States. wiki.content: Californication is the seventh studio album by American alternative rock band Red Hot Chili Peppers, released on June 8, 1999 on Warner Bros. Records. Produced by Rick Rubin, Californication marked the return of John Frusciante, who had previously appeared on Mother's Milk and Blood Sugar Sex Magik, to replace Dave Navarro as the band's guitarist. Frusciante's return was credited with changing the band's sound altogether. The record was a notable shift in style from what was produced with Navarro. The album's subject material incorporated various sexual innuendos commonly associated with the band, and introduced themes of lust, death, contemplations of suicide, and drugs. Californication produced several hits for the band, including "Otherside", "Californication" and the Grammy Award-winning "Scar Tissue". Californication peaked at number three on the U.S. Billboard 200. It is the Chili Peppers' most commercially successful album to date, selling more than fifteen million copies worldwide; a revitalization in comparison to their previous album, One Hot Minute. The record marked a change in style for the band; Rolling Stone's Greg Tate noted that "while all previous Chili Peppers projects have been highly spirited, Californication dares to be spiritual and epiphanic." After their 1995 release One Hot Minute, the Red Hot Chili Peppers released Californication, which saw them reclaiming their extreme notoriety among the alternative rock fraternity. John Frusciante returned to the band in 1998 after leaving in 1992, replacing Dave Navarro as the guitarist. Navarro, of Jane's Addiction, gave the band a heavy, psychedelic sound; Frusciante brought back with him the melodic 'punk funk' that had helped bring the band to stardom. Californication gained positive critical acceptance in contrast to its less popular predecessor, One Hot Minute, and was a greater success worldwide. Rolling Stone credited Kiedis for his drastically improved vocals: " vocal cords have apparently been down to some crossroads and over the rehab, and returned with heretofore unheard-of range, body, pitch, soulfulness, and melodic sensibility." Songs such as "Otherside" and "Porcelain" were called "Pumpkins-esque", while the album as a whole was "epiphanal" and that the "RHCP furthermuckers are now moving toward funk's real Holy Grail: that salty marriage of esoteric mythology and insatiable musicality that salvages souls, binds communities and heals the sick." Other critics credited the album's success to the return of Frusciante. Allmusic's Greg Prato said that the "obvious reason for rebirth is the reappearance of guitarist John Frusciante", considering him to be the "quintessential RHCP guitarist". The album as a whole was "a bona fide Chili Peppers classic". Entertainment Weekly also credits Frusciante with transforming the band's sound into a "more relaxed, less grating, and, in their own way, more introspective album than ever before". Mark Woodlief of Ray Gun commented that "'This Velvet Glove' strikes an intricate balance between a lush acoustic guitar foundation and anthemic rock," Woodlief continued "the disco intro to 'Parallel Universe' gives way to a scorching Western giddy-up motif in the chorus, and Frusciante's Hendrix-like excursions at the song's close." While many critics found the band's new sound refreshing, NME criticized the Chili Peppers for rarely utilizing their trademark funk sound, asking: "Can we have our brain-dead, half-dressed funk-hop rock animals back now, please? All this false empathy is starting to make my removed rib tingle." Pitchfork, while considering the album a triumph over One Hot Minute, felt Californication lacked the funk that was ever-present in Blood Sugar Sex Magik. It went on to scrutinize some lyrics for being overly sexual, but also considered Frusciante to be "the best big-time American rock guitarist going right now." The album received criticism for what Tim Anderson of The Guardian called "excessive compression and distortion" in the process of digital mastering. Stylus Magazine labeled it as one of the victims of the loudness war and commented that it suffered from digital clipping so much that "even non-audiophile consumers complained about it". An unmastered bootleg has been circulated around the internet. Loudness War Waveform of bootlegged "unmastered" version (top) versus waveform of original CD release (bottom), scaled to show relative volume levels. Over the years, Californication has maintained its popularity. "Scar Tissue" won a Grammy award for best rock song in 2000. The album was ranked number 399 on Rolling Stone Magazine's 2003 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time and, in 2006, the Chili Peppers recorded a five-set playlist for AOL Sessions that included "Scar Tissue" and "Californication". The album produced many staple hits for the Chili Peppers; five of the sixteen songs on their Greatest Hits album were taken from Californication. Immediately following the release of Californication, the band embarked on a world tour to support the record, beginning in the United States. To culminate the US leg of their tour, the Chili Peppers were asked to close Woodstock '99, which became infamous for the violence it resulted in. The band was informed minutes before arriving that the crowds and bonfires in the fields had gone out of control. When the Chili Peppers performed a tribute to Jimi Hendrix's song "Fire" to finish their set as a favour to Hendrix's sister, the disruption escalated into violence when several women who had been crowd surfing and moshing were raped and nearby property was looted and destroyed. Kiedis felt that "It was clear that this situation had nothing to do with Woodstock anymore. It wasn't symbolic of peace and love, but of greed and cashing in... We woke up to papers and radio stations vilifying us for playing 'Fire'." To kick off the band's European tour, the band staged a free show in Moscow's Red Square, on August 14, 1999, to a crowd of over 200,000. Kiedis recalled the situation: "Red Square was so filled with wall-to-wall Russians that we needed a police escort to get near the stage." Following the European leg, the group did a show in New York City, at the Windows on the World, for KROQ radio contest-winners, and then at the Big Day Out festival in Australia following several Japanese tour dates. Flea, however, began to feel the repercussions of touring causing the band to set up concerts that were less strenuous, and consequently less financially rewarding, for them. These shows would finish the remainder of the Californication tour. As one of the last shows before the release of their next album "By the Way, the Chili Peppers played Rock in Rio 3." wiki.content: Hybrid Theory is the debut album by the American rock band Linkin Park, released on October 24th, 2000 through Warner Bros. Records. The album was a huge commercial success, selling over 10 million units in the United States alone and peaking at number two on the Billboard 200 while also reaching high positions on other charts worldwide, despite receiving mixed reviews from publications. It has also sold 24 million copies worldwide as of 2009, including over 10 million in the U.S. which makes it the band's best-selling album, the second best-selling album of the 21st century so far, and the second best selling debut album. It is also one of the few albums to be certified Diamond in the U.S. that was released in this century. Recorded at NRG Recordings in North Hollywood, California, and produced by Don Gilmore, the album's lyrical themes deal with problems lead vocalist Chester Bennington experienced during his adolescence, including drug abuse and the constant fighting and divorce of his parents. Hybrid Theory takes its title from the previous name of the band. Four singles were released from the album: "One Step Closer", "Papercut", "In the End", and the Grammy Award-winning "Crawling", which along with "In the End" was responsible for launching Linkin Park into mainstream popularity. At the 2002 Grammy Awards, Hybrid Theory was nominated for Best Rock Album. Hybrid Theory was released in the United States on October 24th, 2000 following the debut of "One Step Closer" on the radio. It entered the U.S. Billboard 200 charts at #16 in late 2000, and was certified gold by the RIAA five weeks after its release. In 2001, Hybrid Theory sold 4.8 million copies in the United States, making it the best-selling album of the year, and it was estimated that the album continued selling 100,000 copies per week in early 2002. Throughout the following years, the album continued to sell at a fast pace and was certified diamond by the RIAA in 2005 for selling 10 million copies in the U.S. In 2007, it has sold over 10 million copies in the U.S. alone. It has also sold 24 million copies worldwide as of 2009, including over 10 million in the U.S. which makes it the band's best-selling album and the best-selling debut album of the 21st century. Critical opinion for Hybrid Theory was mixed. Some critics gave the album positive reviews; Stephanie Dickison of PopMatters commented that the band was a "far more complex and talented group than the hard rock boy bands of late", and claimed that "they will continue to fascinate and challenge music's standard sounds." Q magazine gave Hybrid Theory four out of five stars. Robert Christgau of The Village Voice wrote that “the men don't know what the angry boys understand”, and gave the album a "two-star honorable mention rating", citing "Papercut" and "Points of Authority" as highlights of the album. Jenny Eliscu of Rolling Stone commented that Hybrid Theory had "as much potency as albums by Limp Bizkit or Korn" and called it an album that "reflects the frustration of life". Other critics, however, dismissed the album. Allmusic writer William Ruhlmann said that "Linkin Park sounds like a Johnny-come-lately to an already overdone musical style" and called "One Step Closer" "a typical effort", referring to the lyrics of the song's chorus. NME's Noel Gardner commented that "otherwise damn fine soaring emo-crunchers like 'With You' and 'A Place for My Head' are pointlessly jazzed up with tokenistic scratching," giving the album a score of six out of ten. Despite initially mixed reviews, Hybrid Theory found itself in several “must have” lists that were compiled by various music publications, networks, and other media. Some of the more prominent of these lists to feature Hybrid Theory are shown below: Publication Accolade Rank The Village Voice Pazz & Jop 159 Classic Rock The 100 Greatest Rock Albums of All-Time 72 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame The Definitive 200 64 Esli Jacinth 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die* Record Collector Best of 2001* Rock Sound Les 150 Albums De La Génération (Top 150 Albums of Our Lifetime)58 Read more on Last.fm.
